newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU weighs sparing U.S. and others food safety law.
newsitem.headline: EU weighs sparing U.S. and others food safety law.

text.p: The European Commission, facing a possible transatlantic trade dispute, is studying whether the United States could be exempted from a new meat safety law which will ban use of certain animal byproducts such as tallow.

A European Union source said on Friday the bloc's Brussels-based executive body was examining a request from Washington, along with similar demands from Australia, New Zealand and Canada, to be spared the new law because they were free of mad cow disease.
The requests will be considered in September by the EU's Scientific Veterinary Committee, which will at the same time consider tightening up the rules, the source said.

Earlier a spokeswoman for U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said Washington could take the 15-nation bloc to the World Trade Organisation over the new directive, which the EU plans to implement on January 1.
"We have expressed our concern to the EU concerning the directive," the spokeswoman said in Washington. "If they don't change the directive, we'll take them to the WTO."

She said the new rules -- aimed at controlling the spread of mad cow disease by banning the parts of cattle most likely to carry the disease from entering the food chain -- would have a "severe negative impact" on U.S. exports.

In addition to affecting beef tallow producers, the directive has major consequences for pharmaceuticals and cosmetics manufacturers, since tallow derivatives are used in a wide variety of those products.

To be exempted from the law, the EU source -- speaking on condition of anonymity -- said the country concerned must prove there was "negligeable risk" not only of transmitting mad cow disease, but also other "transmissible spongiform encephalopathy" (TSE) diseases such as scrapie.
The September meeting of the EU scientific committee will also consider "fine-tuning" the EU law, which was narrowly agreed by EU farm ministers on July 23, the source said.

That fine-tuning will involve looking at the kind of tissues included in the directive, and examining whether the age of the cattle covered, currently standing at 12 months and more, should be lowered, he said.
The EU source said that the bloc was not seeking to send out panic signals about the safety of cosmetics, but that it was erring on the safe side as a potential risk had been identified.

He pointed to New Guinea, where women traditionally rub themselves with the ashes of dead relatives. Tests had revealed higher incidences in women of the TSE disease kuru, suggesting that the illness can be transmitted throught the skin.
Last year the mad cow consumer scare blew up when British health officials announced a possible connection between the disease and a similar human brain disease.
